reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: Sesamoiditis is pain and inflammation of the hallucal sesamoids beneath the first metatarsal head, usually from repetitive overload rather than a single injury
The two sesamoids are embedded within the flexor hallucis brevis tendon and act as a pulley and load-bearing cushion for the great toe, so they take high force at push-off
Pain is localised to the plantar aspect of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, worse on weight bearing, dorsiflexion of the great toe, and push-off, and eased by rest
The medial (tibial) sesamoid is more often affected because it bears greater load, and focal plantar tenderness over one sesamoid is characteristic
It is common in runners, dancers, and those in high-heeled or hard-soled footwear, and is favoured by a cavus foot or plantarflexed first ray
Radiographs including an axial sesamoid view help, but a bipartite sesamoid can mimic a fracture, and MRI or bone scan distinguishes stress injury, osteonecrosis, and fracture
Distinguish it from sesamoid stress fracture, osteonecrosis, osteoarthritis, turf toe, and gout

Management is largely conservative with offloading orthoses and a sesamoid cut-out or metatarsal pad, stiff-soled footwear, activity modification, and taping, with corticosteroid injection or sesamoidectomy reserved for resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: The hallucal sesamoids are two small bones enclosed within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis on the plantar surface of the first metatarsal head, where they increase the mechanical advantage of the flexor, absorb load, and protect the flexor hallucis longus tendon. During push-off the great toe dorsiflexes and the sesamoids are drawn distally and loaded heavily, so repetitive high forces, as in running, dancing, and jumping, or sustained pressure from hard or high-heeled footwear, produce an overload inflammation of the sesamoid and its surrounding soft tissues. A cavus foot or a plantarflexed first ray increases the load borne by the sesamoids and predisposes to symptoms. Persistent overload may progress to a stress reaction or stress fracture, and impaired blood supply can lead to osteonecrosis, while a congenitally bipartite sesamoid can be a source of confusion on imaging and a site of symptomatic stress.
additionalDifferentials: Sesamoid stress fracture or acute fracture
Turf toe injury of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Hallux rigidus or hallux valgus with plantar symptoms
Plantar soft-tissue lesion or interdigital neuroma
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination with focal palpation of the tibial and fibular sesamoids and pain on great-toe dorsiflexion
Weight-bearing foot radiographs including an axial (sesamoid) view
MRI to differentiate stress reaction, fracture, osteonecrosis, and inflammation
Bone scan where MRI is unavailable or a stress injury is suspected
Assessment of foot type for cavus or a plantarflexed first ray
Serum urate if gout is a consideration
Pedobarography to assess loading beneath the first ray where relevant
redFlags: Acute severe plantar pain after a hyperextension injury suggesting fracture or a turf toe with sesamoid disruption
A hot, red, swollen joint suggesting gout or infection
Progressive pain with imaging changes suggesting osteonecrosis or established stress fracture
Rest or night pain or a destructive lesion suggesting infection or tumour
reference.prognosis: Most cases of overload sesamoiditis settle with offloading, footwear modification, and activity reduction, though recovery can be slow because the sesamoids are heavily loaded with every step. Stress fractures and osteonecrosis take longer and occasionally fail to heal, and sesamoidectomy usually relieves pain but can alter first-ray mechanics and, if both sesamoids are removed, cause deformity, so it is reserved for resistant cases.
pitfalls: Mistaking a bipartite sesamoid for a fracture, or vice versa, on plain radiographs
Attributing plantar first metatarsophalangeal pain to sesamoiditis while missing a stress fracture or osteonecrosis
Removing both sesamoids and creating a cock-up or clawing deformity of the great toe
Overlooking a cavus foot or plantarflexed first ray that perpetuates sesamoid overload
Missing gout or infection as the cause of an acutely inflamed joint
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Offload the sesamoids with relative rest, activity modification, and avoidance of high-heeled or hard-soled footwear
Cushioned insoles or orthoses with a sesamoid cut-out or metatarsal padding to redistribute load away from the first metatarsal head
Simple analgesia and NSAIDs for pain and inflammation
Taping or a stiff-soled shoe or walker boot to limit great-toe dorsiflexion during healing
Physiotherapy and graded return to activity, correcting a cavus foot or plantarflexed first ray with orthoses
Monitor for progression to stress fracture or osteonecrosis with repeat imaging if pain persists despite offloading
Refer for orthopaedic or podiatric opinion and consider sesamoidectomy for refractory disease, non-union, or osteonecrosis
